article_title: Is using artificial intelligence tools for academic work cheating? Student perceptions, ethics, and the impact
citation: Padhy, A. (2026). Is using artificial intelligence tools for academic work cheating? Student perceptions, ethics, and the impact on academic performance and critical thinking. International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability, 2(2), 919-942. https://doi.org/10.70593/deepsci.0202038
title: Higher education should establish concrete ethical standards, encourage AI literacy, and reshape assessment to foster human-AI collaboration without compromising originality, equity, and intellectual growth
description: The review's forward-looking design recommendation is a three-part institutional response to AI in academic work: formulating concrete ethical standards, encouraging AI literacy, and reshaping assessment methods. It argues these should "foster Human-AI Collaboration without compromising originality, equity, and intellectual growth". The principle positions institutional policy and assessment design, rather than prohibition, as the appropriate response to student AI use.
requirements: Institutional commitment to formulating concrete ethical standards and to assessment redesign
target_learners: higher education students
university instructors and administrators
target_learning_goals: ethical use of AI in academic work
originality and intellectual growth in assessment
examples: The review concludes that reshaping assessment methods and encouraging AI literacy are needed to support human-AI collaboration in higher education
key_sources: Padhy, A. (2026). Is using artificial intelligence tools for academic work cheating? Student perceptions, ethics, and the impact on academic performance and critical thinking. International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability, 2(2), 919-942. https://doi.org/10.70593/deepsci.0202038

article_title: Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students
citation: Buket Bilgiç and Demet Sever (2026). Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00601-0
title: Researcher-developed Likert-type surveys on ethical AI use for students and faculty members
description: The study's quantitative phase used Likert-type surveys prepared separately for students and faculty members to measure views on ethical AI use in education. Both surveys showed high internal consistency ("students: α = 0.906, ω = 0.906; faculty members: α = 0.948, ω = 0.952"). Exploratory factor analysis yielded a four-factor structure for the student survey explaining 38.00% of total variance and a five-factor structure for the faculty survey explaining 56.33%. The instruments were developed by the researchers and revised through expert review and pilot applications before use.
requirements: All data collection tools were developed by the researchers and revised through expert review and pilot applications.
constraints: The article states that additional analyses are required for the instrument to be considered a validated scale.
target_learners: higher education students
faculty members
target_learning_goals: assessing perspectives on the ethical use of AI in higher education
examples: The surveys were administered under stratified sampling by academic unit, with responses analyzed descriptively in JAMOVI.
key_sources: Buket Bilgiç and Demet Sever (2026). Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00601-0

article_title: Ethics Training Agents: Facilitating Group-Based Ethics Education with Role-Playing and Discussion for Ethical Reflection and Exploration
citation: Seo, Y., Jang, S., Park, H., Gutierrez, R. S., Seering, J., & Lee, U. (2026). Ethics Training Agents: Facilitating Group-Based Ethics Education with Role-Playing and Discussion for Ethical Reflection and Exploration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11529
title: Ethics Training Agents: multi-human multi-agent LLM discussion system for ethics education
description: Ethics Training Agents is a web-based group discussion system that "leverages multiple LLM participants embodying distinct ethical orientations, along with a moderator agent, to enable structured human-AI group ethical discussions for collaborative reflection." Built on the Judgment Call tabletop game, it implements four discussion stages (Identify Stakeholders, Write Reviews, Identify Problems, Find Solutions) using GPT-4o-based agents with care ethics, deontological ethics, and pragmatic ethics personas. The system includes a facilitator agent managing flow control, summarization, and idea selection.
requirements: Requires GPT-4o or comparable LLM, a web client, WebSocket server, and agent orchestration module using LangGraph
Designed for groups of three human participants plus three LLM agent participants in a 3:3 configuration
constraints: Activity constrained to approximately 75 minutes to fit a single university class session
Temperature set to 0 for all agents to minimize hallucination and cross-session variability
Agent message length capped at 150 characters with speech-bubble splitting
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM students with sufficient coursework experience in technology design
examples: 45 undergraduate STEM students in 15 groups of three discussed a Black Mirror smart lens scenario across four structured stages with three LLM persona agents and one facilitator agent
key_sources: Seo, Y., Jang, S., Park, H., Gutierrez, R. S., Seering, J., & Lee, U. (2026). Ethics Training Agents: Facilitating Group-Based Ethics Education with Role-Playing and Discussion for Ethical Reflection and Exploration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11529

article_title: Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting
citation: Freyaa Chawla, Ahan Chawla, Rishi Singh, Joe Germino, Grigorii Khvatskii. (2026). Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05144
title: Student-built ETF forecasting pipeline with LLM-scored news sentiment dataset
description: The project's technical artifact is a two-stage predictive system: regression models estimate the magnitude of ETF price deltas and classification models predict direction, with predictions merged by multiplying magnitude and sign. The dataset covers "a historical price dataset for 29 exchange-traded funds (ETFs), covering January 2, 2024 through September 23, 2025" harvested via the Yahoo Finance API, plus 260 scraped NASDAQ news articles scored by gpt-5-mini on a -10 to +10 scale with justifications, aggregated daily by sector. Sentiment coverage was sparse and uneven across ETFs, from 0% to 23.16% as shown in Table 1.
requirements: Mentor intervention was needed for rate limiting, error recovery, and anti-bot scraping measures such as dynamic content loading.
constraints: Sector-level sentiment aggregation may dilute ETF-specific signals; zero-imputation for days without news may introduce bias; LLM scores were not validated against human-coded ground truth.
target_learners: high-school students
early-undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: working with APIs and structured financial data
machine learning model development and validation
examples: Automated visualizations were generated for each ETF, overlaying predicted and actual price movements alongside sentiment trends to facilitate comparative analysis and interpretation.
key_sources: Freyaa Chawla, Ahan Chawla, Rishi Singh, Joe Germino, Grigorii Khvatskii. (2026). Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05144

article_title: When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education
citation: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237
title: Address privacy, equity, academic integrity, transparency, and overreliance when integrating GAI across its roles
description: The article argues that responsible GAI adoption in marketing education requires addressing a set of ethical considerations spanning its three roles. These "encompass privacy, equity, academic integrity, transparency, and potential overreliance on AI systems, each requiring careful attention to ensure responsible implementation." Educators must establish clear data-handling protocols compliant with regulations like FERPA and develop inclusive implementation strategies so all students can benefit regardless of technological or economic circumstances.
requirements: Clear protocols for data handling and student privacy
Inclusive implementation strategies addressing the digital divide in access to GAI tools
constraints: Premium GAI service costs and limited technology infrastructure can create disparities; existing biases in GAI systems may disadvantage certain student groups
target_learners: all students in GAI-integrated marketing courses
target_learning_goals: responsible and equitable use of GAI in learning
examples: Institutions with privacy-preserving infrastructure make faculty GAI use easier; otherwise instructors must give students clear guidelines on privacy-preserving use of public GAI technologies; several providers offer free access and open-source models with comparable capabilities
key_sources: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Ethics-of-care redefinition of connectedness as a demand-driven, two-way, responsive process
description: The article redefines connectedness as 'A relational experience of demand satisfaction formed by subjects engaging in caring interactions with other beings based on genuine needs, via two-way investment and reciprocal responsive confirmation.' It claims three advances over prior definitions: the logical starting point shifts from emotion to demand identification, one-sided perception becomes two-way mutual investment, and the value of connectedness becomes demand satisfaction and self-confirmation rather than mere anxiety reduction. The construct is grounded in Noddings' care practice of engrossment, motivational displacement, and reciprocal response confirmation, and explicitly incorporates ethical questions about who defines needs and bears responsibility for response.
requirements: Connectedness must be understood as generated through a cyclic mechanism of need identification, behavioral investment, and responsive confirmation rather than as a static relational state.
target_learners: adolescents
examples: The article contrasts its definition with Hagerty et al.'s human relatedness theory, which explains associative states through four relatedness capacity elements without deconstructing the generative mechanism of connectedness.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: A Systematic Review Mapping of AI Literacy Progression in K–12
citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Provide ethical training to every student learning AI, computer science, or data science, augmented with technical tools and methods for preventing unacceptable outcomes
description: The report recommends that ethical training for AI practitioners and students is a necessary part of the solution to AI's fairness and safety challenges. It states that "Ideally, every student learning AI, computer science, or data science would be exposed to curriculum and discussion on related ethics and security topics." It adds that ethics alone is not sufficient and "ethical training should be augmented with technical tools and methods for putting good intentions into practice."
requirements: Curriculum and discussion on ethics and security topics must be available to students learning AI, computer science, or data science, per the report's recommendation
constraints: The report states ethics alone is not sufficient: ethical training should be augmented with technical tools and methods
target_learners: students learning AI, computer science, or data science
target_learning_goals: understanding ethical and security responsibilities of AI practitioners
putting good intentions into practice through technical work
examples: The report's Fairness, Safety, and Governance section recommends exposing every AI, computer science, or data science student to ethics and security curriculum and discussion

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Ethnomethodology as epistemic framing for CSCL research
description: Stahl situates ethnomethodology (EM) as a foundational epistemic orientation for CSCL, defining CSCL as the study of joint meaning and grounding CSCL in EM's explicit study of those methods. This defines CSCL's rational grounding in ethnography, where EM defines attention to methods of intersubjectivity, and links CSCL to conversation analysis as a strand of EM focused on sequential analysis of interaction.
requirements: Sufficient temporal granularity of interaction data (logs, recordings, or transcripts) to support sequential microanalysis of group cognition
constraints: EM case studies use situated, non-generalizable analyses rather than controlled experiments; designed artifacts and collaboration practices must be analyzed from within members' rather than analysts' terminology
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning methods of intersubjectivity and joint meaning making
examples: Stahl links Koschmann's foundational CSCL framing to Garfinkel's ethnomethodology and conversation analysis as an exemplar EM method
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Etic–emic distinction applied to school belonging: Western-derived definitions may not capture culture-specific meanings
description: The commentary argues that much belonging research adopts "an etic approach, which involves testing concepts developed in Western psychology across different cultural groups", applying Goodenow and Grady's Western-derived definition globally through translated instruments that assume conceptual equivalence. Emic approaches, by contrast, ask students how they understand belonging, exclusion, and acceptance in their own contexts. The commentary cites Li's (2003) prototype analysis—Americans view learning primarily as cognitive while Chinese students associate it with social and moral development—as a model of what etic instruments miss.
requirements: In-depth qualitative studies across diverse cultural contexts to uncover both etic commonalities and emic variations
constraints: The commentary presents this as an argument for future research; no new emic belonging data are collected here
target_learners: Students in non-WEIRD and marginalized cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Culturally valid conceptualization and measurement of school belonging
examples: Saravi et al. (2020) developed an emic understanding of belonging among disadvantaged Mexican students, showing stigmatization and institutional practices shape belonging in ways WEIRD-dominated research seldom captures
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Special issue on cognition and learning technology
citation: J. Michael Spector. (2010). Special issue on cognition and learning technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9149-2
title: ETR&D special issue on Cognition and Learning Technology (2010)
description: A journal special issue of Education Tech Research Dev devoted to cognition and learning technology, edited for issue 57(6) but ultimately spread across multiple issues. It includes papers such as "A Feedback Learning and Mental Models Perspective on Strategic Decision Making" by Carlos Capelo and João Ferreira Dias and "Highly Integrated Model Assessment Technology and Tools" by Pablo Pirnay-Dummer, Dirk Ifenthaler, and J. Michael Spector. The editorial notes the collection was "originally scheduled to appear in the last issue of 2009—57(6)".
requirements: Readers seeking the full special issue must consult multiple issues of ETR&D (57(5), 57(6), and 58(1)) rather than a single issue
target_learners: researchers and practitioners in educational technology and learning sciences
target_learning_goals: understanding the relationship between cognition and learning technology as covered by the special issue's papers
examples: The final special-issue paper, "Highly Integrated Model Assessment Technology and Tools" by Pirnay-Dummer, Ifenthaler, and Spector, appears in issue 58(1).

article_title: Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study
citation: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6
title: Three socio-cultural perspectives inform social justice in learning design: ethical, cultural, and critical
description: The article organizes socio-cultural approaches to learning design around three perspectives. An ethical perspective involves "making judgements about what learners need" based on rules and normative commitments; a cultural perspective attends to learners' and teams' cultures, values, and norms during design; a critical perspective examines how "power dynamics and social structures impact people's lived experiences" and are reproduced through designed materials. The study uses these perspectives to characterize each case's approach to centering social justice.
requirements: Designers must consider who they are in relation to those they work with and the societal impact of their designs
constraints: The article notes limited guidance on how to apply these perspectives toward social justice goals
target_learners: Learning designers and LDT scholars
target_learning_goals: Designing learning experiences that address equity, inclusion, and power in socio-cultural context
examples: Case 1 took an ethical perspective guided by an institutional DEI framework; Cases 2 and 4 took cultural perspectives; Case 3 took a critical perspective amplifying marginalized voices.
key_sources: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6

article_title: Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners' Comprehension and Retention of Idioms
citation: Bagheri, M. S., & Fazel, I. (2010). Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners’ Comprehension and Retention of Idioms. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 14(1), 45-55. https://www.paaljapan.org
title: Etymological elaboration technique for teaching idioms
description: Etymological elaboration (EE) is the technique of "associating the meaning of idioms with their original, literal usage" (attributed by the article to Boers, Demecheleer & Eyckmans, 2004). In this study it was operationalized as a matching exercise in which learners matched 15 idioms to their origins, received an answer key, and could not change their answers. The article treats it as a novel, appealing way of learning and teaching idioms in classroom settings.
requirements: Learners are provided with the origins or original literal usage of the idioms, followed by an answer key for checking.
constraints: Tested only with advanced (IELTS 5–6) Persian-speaking EFL adults aged 18–22 on 15 idioms replicated from Boers et al. (2007).
target_learners: Intermediate-to-advanced EFL learners
examples: The experimental group's test comprised a matching task on idiom origins, a multiple-choice definition task, and a delayed gap-filling task.
key_sources: Bagheri, M. S., & Fazel, I. (2010). Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners’ Comprehension and Retention of Idioms. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 14(1), 45-55. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ920503

article_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study. NCEE 2010-4027
citation: Glazerman, S., E. Isenberg, S. Dolfin, M. Bleeker, A. Johnson, M. Grider, and M. Jacobus. (2010). Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results From a Randomized Controlled Study (NCEE 2010-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: ETS and NTC comprehensive teacher induction programs
description: Two comprehensive induction programs, provided by the Educational Testing Service (ETS) and the New Teacher Center at the University of California, Santa Cruz (NTC), delivered intensive, structured support to beginning teachers in treatment schools. Support "is often delivered through experienced, trained full-time mentors" and includes orientation sessions, professional development, classroom observations, and formative assessment feedback. Beginning teachers were assigned full-time mentors at a 12 to 1 ratio, mentors received ongoing training and a curriculum of materials, and teachers received monthly professional development sessions, opportunities to observe veteran teachers, and an end-of-year colloquium.
requirements: Carefully selected and trained full-time mentors
a curriculum of intensive and structured support including orientation, professional development, and weekly mentor meetings
formative assessment tools permitting ongoing evaluation of practice
outreach to district and school-based administrators for systemic support
constraints: Districts in the study had no existing comprehensive induction program, no full-time mentors, and induction expenditure under $1,000 per beginning teacher
the two sets of districts were not randomly chosen to receive one or two years of treatment
target_learners: beginning elementary teachers (grades K-6) new to the profession in urban districts
target_learning_goals: effective teaching practices in literacy and general instruction
examples: Treatment teachers met weekly with mentors for approximately two hours, attended monthly professional development sessions, observed veteran teachers once or twice a year, and participated in an end-of-year colloquium
key_sources: Glazerman, S., E. Isenberg, S. Dolfin, M. Bleeker, A. Johnson, M. Grider, and M. Jacobus. (2010). Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results From a Randomized Controlled Study (NCEE 2010-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: The impact of ethnicity information in single best answer questions on student performance, item response time and psychometric properties.
citation: Mohan Jenanan, Pishia Michaela, Alim Duaa, McGown Patrick J., Amin Anjali, Pinder Richard J., Halse Omid, Brown Celia, Sam Amir H. (2025). The impact of ethnicity information in single best answer questions on student performance, item response time and psychometric properties. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10489-6
title: Ethnicity in exam stems may act as a cue or distraction that steers diagnostic reasoning toward or away from stereotypically associated conditions
description: The article draws on a content-analysis account of how race functions in question banks: "race was often used either as a deliberate 'clue', such as specifying a patient is black to hint at hypertension-related complications, or as a 'distraction' that steered students toward a stereotypical but incorrect diagnosis" (attributed to Cerdeña et al., 2021). The article uses this framework to interpret its own item-level facility shifts, including a hypertension item made easier and a pleural effusion item made harder by ethnicity cues.
requirements: Item writers must consider whether ethnicity in a stem is clinically relevant or merely a cue.
constraints: The article notes the traditional use of ethnicity purely as a diagnostic cue may encourage automaticity and reinforce stereotypes.
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
examples: A hypertension item showed an 11 pp facility increase with ethnicity included, consistent with a clinically relevant clue.
key_sources: Mohan Jenanan, Pishia Michaela, Alim Duaa, McGown Patrick J., Amin Anjali, Pinder Richard J., Halse Omid, Brown Celia, Sam Amir H. (2025). The impact of ethnicity information in single best answer questions on student performance, item response time and psychometric properties. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10489-6

article_title: The Relationship Between Nurses' Ethical Behaviours for Protecting Patients' Rights and Patient-Centred Care Competencies: A Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Ozturk Melek Aksut, Oner Beratiye. (2026). The Relationship Between Nurses' Ethical Behaviours for Protecting Patients' Rights and Patient‐Centred Care Competencies: A Cross‐Sectional Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70744
title: Conceptual framework positioning ethical nursing behaviour protecting patient rights as an enabler of PCC competencies
description: The article proposes an integrative framework in which ethical principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence) inform ethical sensitivity and climate, which shape nurses' ethical behaviours; these behaviours foster PCC competencies such as shared decision-making, individualized care, empathy, and respect. The article states that "nurses' ethical behaviours that protect patients' rights serve as the foundational drivers of PCC competencies such as shared decision‐making, individualized care, and patient advocacy". Demographics and professional experience are treated as moderating factors. It was developed from prior integrative models (Scholl et al. 2014; Entwistle and Watt 2013; Milliken 2018; Schluter et al. 2008; Donkers et al. 2021).
requirements: Ethical principles must be operationalized as observable behaviours protecting patient rights
constraints: The framework's associations are cross-sectional and self-report based; causal direction not established
target_learners: nurses in inpatient and outpatient care settings
key_sources: Ozturk Melek Aksut, Oner Beratiye. (2026). The Relationship Between Nurses' Ethical Behaviours for Protecting Patients' Rights and Patient‐Centred Care Competencies: A Cross‐Sectional Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70744

article_title: European training requirements in geriatric medicine 2025: driving competency-based education and harmonisation across Europe.
citation: Romero Ortuño R, van Iersel M, Nuotio MS, Kolk H, Topinková E, Schoevaerdts D, Farré Mercadé MV, Graf C, Cotobal Rodeles S, Vassallo MA, Vassallo M, Lütje D, Macijauskienė J, on behalf of the UEMS Geriatric Medicine Section (UEMS-GMS). (2026). European training requirements in geriatric medicine 2025: driving competency-based education and harmonisation across Europe. European Geriatric Medicine 17(2):417–428. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-025-01393-8
title: The European Training Requirements (ETR) framework defines minimum standards for competency-based postgraduate specialist education
description: The ETRs are European instruments developed under the UEMS that define common frameworks and minimum standards for postgraduate specialist education. They rest on the premise that "the quality of medical care is directly proportional to the quality of medical training" and are grounded in the CanMEDS framework, in which the physician integrates complementary roles. They are updated approximately every five years and set minimum requirements adaptable to national contexts. The 2025 Geriatric Medicine ETR is presented as a coherent, evidence-informed standard promoting harmonisation, mobility and comparability of training.
requirements: Developed by professionals, for professionals, through the official UEMS procedures, with stakeholder consultation and endorsement by European partner organisations
constraints: They do not constitute legal directives themselves
They encourage adoption or adaptation rather than uniform prescription
target_learners: postgraduate medical trainees in geriatric medicine
target_learning_goals: professional mobility and comparability of training across Europe
examples: The 2025 ETR for Geriatric Medicine was approved unanimously by the UEMS Council in Tbilisi on 17–18 October 2025 and published on the UEMS website
key_sources: Romero Ortuño R, van Iersel M, Nuotio MS, Kolk H, Topinková E, Schoevaerdts D, Farré Mercadé MV, Graf C, Cotobal Rodeles S, Vassallo MA, Vassallo M, Lütje D, Macijauskienė J, on behalf of the UEMS Geriatric Medicine Section (UEMS-GMS). (2026). European training requirements in geriatric medicine 2025: driving competency-based education and harmonisation across Europe. European Geriatric Medicine 17(2):417–428. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-025-01393-8

article_title: Preliminary insights on high-fidelity embalming solutions for surgical skills training-An evaluation using the McMaster Embalming Scale and mechanical tests.
citation: Darie S., Wainman B.C., Wohl G.R., Wang A.Y., Zhang B.Z., Li A., Ahmad E., Palombella A.S., Rockarts J.L., de SA D.L., Nguyen L.N., DeCarlo B., Downer N., Brewer‐Deluce D. (2026). Preliminary insights on high‐fidelity embalming solutions for surgical skills training—An evaluation using the McMaster Embalming Scale and mechanical tests. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70185
title: Select ethanol–phenol as the default soft-embalming solution for surgical skills training programs balancing fidelity with cost, safety, and accessibility
description: The article recommends ethanol–phenol (EP) as the preferred soft-embalming solution for surgical skills training laboratories, based on its combination of fidelity and practical performance. The authors state that "significantly higher suitability ratings of the EP embalmed donor and the midline stability of EP tissues in mechanical testing alongside the modest cost, safety, and availability concerns" make it "a superior choice for use in surgical skills training." The recommendation weighs both tissue performance and laboratory-relevant concerns such as cost per donor and chemical hazards.
requirements: An anatomy laboratory with the capacity to perfuse donors with the ethanol–phenol solution and store embalmed donors at appropriate temperature before testing
constraints: SRF was identified as least recommended due to its proprietary formula and multi-day protocol
SSS required additional technician steps to prevent pump clogging from consolidated sediment
ICL tissue moisture made it read as less life-like, especially for electrocautery
evaluations were made within a 2-week time frame, so stable performance may not persist beyond it
the four donors were not matched on age, sex, or comorbidities, so solution-specific differences could be attributable to donor-specific traits
target_learners: surgical residents (PGY 1–3) in surgical foundations training
target_learning_goals: surgical skills training fidelity: chest tube insertion and anchoring, electrocautery, and bone sawing
examples: EP donors received the highest MES suitability ratings and midline mechanical-test stability across four donors embalmed with SRF, ICL, EP, and SSS
key_sources: Darie S., Wainman B.C., Wohl G.R., Wang A.Y., Zhang B.Z., Li A., Ahmad E., Palombella A.S., Rockarts J.L., de SA D.L., Nguyen L.N., DeCarlo B., Downer N., Brewer‐Deluce D. (2026). article_title: Determinants of effective feedback on educational performance of faculty members based on their own experiences: a content analysis study.
citation: karimijavan Gelavizh, Alizadeh Mahasti, Ranjbar Fatemeh, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Karimi Salah Eddin. (2026). Determinants of effective feedback on educational performance of faculty members based on their own experiences: a content analysis study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08601-4
title: Feedback effectiveness as an ethical-relational process shaped by power, context, and interpersonal trust
description: The article proposes a framework reframing feedback on faculty performance as "an ethical–relational process rather than a purely instructional technique." It integrates individual, relational, and structural factors, arguing that "power dynamics, relational trust, and individual readiness determine effectiveness." Grounded in social cognitive theory, it links individual factors, environment, and behavior, and organizes ten categories into barriers and facilitators of effective feedback in academic settings.
requirements: Feedback effectiveness depends on aligning delivery with the receiver's emotional and cognitive state and on relational trust between giver and receiver
constraints: Derived from faculty experiences at a single Iranian medical university; the authors note this limits generalizability to national or international contexts
target_learners: Faculty members in medical universities
target_learning_goals: Improving effectiveness of feedback on educational performance
examples: The study interviewed 16 faculty members at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences and derived 80 primary codes organized into 10 categories and 2 themes.

article_title: The Active Learning-GenAI Synergy Framework: Ethical Integration of Generative AI in EFL/ESL Writing in Resource-Constrained Contexts.
citation: Rashid S, Malik S, Ghauri F. (2025). The Active Learning–GenAI Synergy Framework: Ethical Integration of Generative AI in EFL/ESL Writing in Resource-Constrained Contexts. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.171435.1
title: Embed generative AI in writing instruction through an Ethical Integration Protocol so collaboration promotes rather than undermines active learning
description: The article's Ethical Integration Protocol combines weekly ethical reflection prompts, academic integrity frameworks distinguishing AI support from AI substitution, critical digital literacy development, and transparency requirements (students disclosed AI use in all submissions). It was "designed to ensure that AI collaboration promoted rather than undermined active learning principles", fostering metacognitive awareness and preventing passive reliance on AI-generated content.
requirements: Weekly structured ethical reflection prompts; explicit integrity guidelines; critical evaluation tasks for AI output quality and bias
constraints: The protocol was implemented in Pakistani undergraduate EFL writing classes; the authors note cross-cultural validation is required
target_learners: Undergraduate EFL/ESL writing students in large, resource-constrained classes
examples: Students completed weekly reflection prompts such that one reported learning "to rewrite and reflect" and appreciating the distinction between AI help and AI substitution

article_title: Evaluating the Value of Eye-Tracking Augmented Debriefing in Medical Simulation-A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Braund H, Hall AK, Caners K, Walker M, Dagnone D, Sherbino J, Sibbald M, Wang B, Howes D, Day AG, Wu W, Szulewski A. (2024). Evaluating the Value of Eye-Tracking Augmented Debriefing in Medical Simulation—A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000825
title: Eye-tracking augmented PEARLS debriefing (ETAD): first-person gaze video as a cueing mechanism within the PEARLS framework
description: ETAD is a debriefing technique in which the debriefer plays back the resident's own first-person video, recorded by eye-tracking glasses with a superimposed gaze indicator, pausing at critical junctures to guide discussion within the PEARLS framework. Debriefers agreed "the video would act as a cueing mechanism to guide directed reflection," with flexibility in its use case by case. Residents were not shown quantitative metrics such as dwell times or pupil size; debriefers cross-referenced automatically generated timestamps with their own notes.
requirements: Requires mobile eye-tracking glasses worn by the learner during the simulation and software that generates timestamped first-person video with gaze overlay
Requires debriefers trained in and consensus on integrating the video into the PEARLS framework
constraints: The article notes practical limitations in implementing ETAD in a teaching setting, including cost and technical challenges
The study tested ETAD only against PEARLS without video, not against first-person video without eye tracking
target_learners: emergency medicine residents in simulation-based resuscitation training
examples: In the trial, experimental-arm residents received an individual 20-minute PEARLS debriefing augmented by their own gaze-overlaid video after each of two resuscitation OSCE stations, while control residents received PEARLS debriefing without video or eye tracking

article_title: The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers.
citation: Laukkanen L, Suhonen R, Löyttyniemi E, Leino-Kilpi H. (2022). The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03241-w
title: Ethics Quarter: a five-dimension, 12-quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers' ethical activity profile
description: The Ethics Quarter (EQ) is an educational ethics e-learning intervention for nurse managers developed at the University of Turku under the CReDECI2 guideline. It has "five dimensions, 12 evidence-based educational quarters, including introduction and summary", covering developing own ethics knowledge, influencing ethical issues, conducting or implementing ethics research, identifying ethical problems, and solving ethical problems. NMs complete two quarters per week over six weeks, with exercises entailing self-reflection and development plans after every dimension. Its pedagogical basis is constructivism, treating NMs as active knowledge constructors who link new knowledge to prior experience.
requirements: Access to the internet is the only requirement for participation
The intervention lasts 6 weeks and requires high engagement
constraints: Developed for nurse managers in Finnish healthcare organizations
Contents must be constantly updated based on the latest knowledge of ethical activities
target_learners: Nurse managers in unit, middle, and strategic level management
examples: Quarters are text material including real-life role model experiences, e.g. NMs' moral courage
key_sources: Laukkanen L, Suhonen R, Löyttyniemi E, Leino-Kilpi H. (2022). The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03241-w

article_title: The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers.
citation: Laukkanen L, Suhonen R, Löyttyniemi E, Leino-Kilpi H. (2022). The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03241-w
title: Ethical activity profile of nurse managers: a five-dimension construct
description: The ethical activity profile of nurse managers is a construct based on previous literature and deductive reasoning, "consisting of five dimensions": developing one's own ethics knowledge, influencing ethical issues, conducting or implementing ethics research, identifying ethical problems, and solving ethical problems. All five dimensions require different types of ethical activities, are equally important, and can be summarized together; a high ethical activity profile requires performing activities from all dimensions. The Ethics Quarter intervention was designed to include all five dimensions.
requirements: To have a high ethical activity profile, NMs have to perform activities from all dimensions
constraints: Based on earlier studies, only a limited number of NMs develop their own ethics knowledge, influence ethical issues, or conduct or implement ethics research
target_learners: Nurse managers responsible for leadership, management and administrative positions in healthcare
target_learning_goals: Performing ethical activities across all five profile dimensions
key_sources: Laukkanen L, Suhonen R, Löyttyniemi E, Leino-Kilpi H. (2022). The usability, feasibility and fidelity of the Ethics Quarter e-learning intervention for nurse managers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03241-w

article_title: Skill Proficiency is Predicted by Intubation Frequency of Emergency Medicine Attending Physicians.
citation: Gillett Brian MD; Saloum David MD, MACM; Aghera Amish MD; Marshall John P. MD, MBA. (2019). Skill Proficiency is Predicted by Intubation Frequency of Emergency Medicine Attending Physicians. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2019.6.42946
title: Novel 11-item checklist plus psychomotor adeptness scale for assessing ETI skill via direct laryngoscopy on a simulator
description: The authors developed a novel assessment tool because no validated DL-based ETI skill tool existed for experienced providers. It combines an 11-item checklist (e.g., "inserts tube to correct depth") with a 0–10 psychomotor adeptness rating of "struggle" defined by "coordination, grace, dexterity, and timing", weighted to a 21-point maximum reported as a percentage. Scores were recorded by consensus of at least two of three pre-trained raters, and internal consistency was good (Cronbach's α = 0.8).
requirements: At least two of three pre-trained raters present, scoring by consensus on a standardized form
A borderline-methods cut score to define proficient performance
constraints: Checklists alone have been criticized for rewarding thoroughness rather than competence, motivating the added global rating scale
No well-established validated tool existed for this population; content validity rests on triangulation of textbooks and expert discussion
target_learners: Board-certified or board-eligible emergency medicine and pediatric emergency medicine attending physicians
target_learning_goals: Endotracheal intubation by direct laryngoscopy procedural skill
examples: Administered individually to 44 attendings on a TruCorp Airsim Advance mannequin as part of a mandated departmental skills advancement initiative
key_sources: Gillett Brian MD; Saloum David MD, MACM; Aghera Amish MD; Marshall John P. MD, MBA. (2019). Skill Proficiency is Predicted by Intubation Frequency of Emergency Medicine Attending Physicians. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2019.6.42946
